extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, journal editors, referees, and scholars of peer review / sociology of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Rubric for making rapid 'quick opinion' judgments of the significance/importance of mathematical research papers (the first-stage screening used by elite journals), distinct from detailed correctness checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance (significance) as a separate axis
rubrics_metrics.description: Score the paper's importance independently from correctness — significance (novelty, impact, generativity, scope) is a distinct dimension of quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greiffenhagen shows community practice separates importance from correctness; design rubrics and processes so importance is judged by quick, experienced reviewers and correctness by detailed referees. Treat importance as a first-stage filter rather than collapsed into a single overall 'quality' score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness (rigor) as a separate axis
rubrics_metrics.description: Score the paper's correctness (rigor, gap-acceptability, internal consistency) independently from importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correctness checking is resource-intensive and typically done in a second stage by referees who line-check proofs. Do not conflate minor gaps with (lack of) importance — an important but flawed paper may merit substantive revision rather than outright rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main theorem statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the main theorem statement answer a recognized open problem or state a clearly meaningful result?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick-opinion readers often read the abstract and main theorem to see whether the claim maps onto known important problems. A clear, well-phrased main theorem that situates itself is a strong signal in a 30-minute quick read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Result strength / improvement over prior work
rubrics_metrics.description: How much stronger is the result relative to prior work? Is it a genuine advance or a marginal extension?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess quantitative improvements (better bounds, weaker hypotheses) and qualitative leaps. Significant improvement over known results is a key indicator for 'important' mathematics; small incremental gains are weaker signals for elite venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique novelty and methodological contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the paper introduce a new method, substantially refine an existing method, or otherwise contribute a technique others will reuse?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique novelty can be as valuable as the specific result; introducing reusable methods increases generativity. Watch for mismatches where heavy machinery is used for an unsurprising result or elementary methods claim to solve deep problems (both are red flags).

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth / cross-area impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Will the result or technique affect multiple subfields, or is it relevant only to a narrow specialty?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results that connect areas or have cross-disciplinary reach score higher for elite-journal importance. Evaluate how many subfields the work is likely to influence and whether it provides tools usable beyond a niche.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's prior work / track record
rubrics_metrics.description: The author's prior contributions in the area are taken as evidence when judging importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senior quick-opinion givers use track record as a signal — well-established researchers with relevant prior work get some positive weight. This is a heuristic, not a substitute for actual significance of the current result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposition quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The clarity and quality of the paper's exposition are taken as positive signals in quick judgments of importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-written papers that present the problem, motivation, and main result clearly make it easier for a quick reader to assess significance; poor exposition can hide importance or be taken as a negative sign in a short read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem setup / problem-recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the problem genuinely interesting to the field (field-recognized), or is it contrived/manufactured?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick-opinion reviewers check whether the problem fits into recognized research trajectories or 'Hilbert-style' programs. If the setup doesn't resonate with acknowledged priorities, that reduces perceived importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection to long-recognized problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the work connect to or resolve problems that the community has long recognized as important?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closing or progressing on well-known open problems is a high signal of importance. Claims of answering named questions should be clearly substantiated; mere name-dropping without substantive connection is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closing a long-open problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolving a longstanding open problem is among the strongest signals of importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviewed editors treat closing long-open problems as the highest-value outcome; use this as a major positive when present, even if correctness needs later checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproving a conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Producing a counterexample or disproving a conjecture is often especially valuable and may outrank 'expected' positive results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disproofs can reshape agendas and are valued highly; verify the novelty of the counterexample and its implications for the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connecting previously separate areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Bridging gaps between subfields or synthesizing methods from different areas is a marker of importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connections that open cross-area dialogue or enable transfer of techniques raise a paper's impact beyond a single subcommunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Producing tools / generative potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the work produce tools, constructions, or methods that can solve adjacent problems and generate new research directions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generativity — the capacity to open new problems and lines of work — is a key criterion; consider whether the paper is likely to spawn follow-up work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the paper settle conceptual/foundational questions or shift conceptual understanding beyond resolving a technical calculation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers that change the conceptual framework of an area (axiomatic or definitional shifts) have deep significance; such conceptual shifts weigh heavily in quick opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvability (room for future work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the result leave room for improvement or does it look like a 'final answer'?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both directions can be valuable: a final striking resolution is important, but results that open many follow-up questions (improvability/gaps) can be generative and thus important. Evaluate whether the paper stimulates further work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage process / division of labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a cheap, fast senior quick-opinion to evaluate importance first; only positively graded papers proceed to slow, detailed correctness refereeing (often by junior referees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This process design rationale: quick opinions take ~30 minutes, correctness checking takes weeks. Align rubric design with this division — separate procedures, different reviewers, and different evaluation criteria for each stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-patterns / red flags in quick-opinion judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators that a paper's claimed importance is suspect: name-dropping without connection; artificially inflated difficulty; mismatch of technique and claim; manufactured subfields; many small theorems instead of one substantive result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick-opinion reviewers watch for these red flags and may mark such submissions as not important. Examples: claiming to answer 'a question of X' without showing relevance; using heavy machinery for trivial outcomes; fragmentary papers packaged as many minor contributions.
